newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Mediators begin Central African Republic dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Mediators begin Central African Republic dialogue.

text.p: African mediators launched a political debate on the future of the Central African Republic on Saturday as a first step towards national reconciliation following ethnic bloodshed and army revolts.
Hundreds of people have died in the conflict, which flared anew on November 15 when a section of the army mutinied for the third time in a year.
Mali's respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, told Central Africans gathered in the national assembly that they had to act quickly to find a peaceful settlement.
"It's necessary to step back, quickly, and to find a peaceful and lasting solution," he told the gathering which was due to name a multi-party conciliation committee.
The mutinies began last April over pay but turned into a campaign to oust President Ange-Felix Patasse, a civilian elected in 1993. A fragile truce runs out on January 23.
Toumani Toure said the military problem could not be addressed without attacking the political problem.
"This is a challenge which demands commitment from all African countries but above all it is a challenge that demands commitment from the Central African Republic and its political class," he said.
A spokesman for Patasse said he did not want to complicate the mediators' task and would join the talks later.

French troops, in the country under a defence pact, control key intersections in the capital's volatile southern suburbs, from which they ejected the mutineers after last Saturday's killing of two French officers on a mediation mission.
Life in the city has resumed the trappings of normality, with markets open and taxis and residents circulating in what were no-go areas, but tension is not far from the surface.
The mutineers, who are from the minority Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba, numbered about 750 but scattered after losing men and territory in French raids last Sunday.

"We must regroup to take stock before we go to the negotiations," the rebels' French-trained spokesman Parfait Mbay told Reuters. He said mutineers had fled to the forest and across the broad Oubangui River into Zaire.
Kassai camp in the east of the city remains in rebel hands.

French commanders say their role is to protect symbols of state authority and foreign nationals, help life return to normal and act as a buffer between mutineers and presidential guard loyalists -- who are bitter rivals.
French intervention last May kept Patasse in power.
French officials say Sunday's retaliatory raids killed 10 mutineers but concede the toll could be higher. The mutineers put the death toll at 32, including 11 civilians.

The heads of state of Mali, Burkina Faso, Gabon and Chad launched the mediation effort in December. They mandated Toumani Toure, who is widely respected for ushering in civilian rule in his native Mali, to broker a lasting deal on their behalf.
